name: Thidranki
summary: The oldest of the proving fields, a farm gone wild around Thidranki Faste, where the tomte and the bwca still quarrel over a household that left (20-24).

facts.text: Thidranki is the battleground for levels 20 to 24 (region 252); level is the only limit in Offline DAoC.
Its central keep is Thidranki Faste; an Albion, a Midgard and a Hibernia portal keep stand at the same three places as in the other battlegrounds.
Thidranki Faste starts neutral in the release world.
Thidranki, Murdaigean and Caledonia were the classic battlegrounds; Abermenai came with patch 1.62 (June 2003).

Its monsters are tomte hunters, soldiers, mystics and visionaries, perturbed bwca, mature boars, rabid and maddened badgers and clicking beetles (levels 19-24). Haluka (24) is a bwca twice the size of the others, by the Hibernia portal keep, and does not wander; the other bwca roam.

facts.text: Thidranki has no Renegade Chieftain or renegade camp in the world data, unlike Abermenai, Murdaigean and Caledon.

facts.text: Each portal keep has named siegemasters: Salendar and Cadman (Albion), Ordrand and Sigfreid (Midgard), Camey and Erinden (Hibernia); Void Merchants trade realm points at the Midgard and Hibernia portal keeps.

facts.text: Tomte are the farm spirits of Swedish folklore and bwca the household spirits of Welsh tradition; both are the spirits of a farmstead.

In Thidranda thattr ok Thorhalls, Thidrandi goes out at a Winter Nights feast against a seer's warning when someone knocks three times; nine women in black ride from the north and kill him, nine in white from the south come too late, and the seer calls them the family's disir.
The tomte is the Scandinavian farm spirit who minds the beasts; the bwca is the Welsh house-spirit who works by night for a bowl of cream.
Thidrand's farm, the two kinds of spirit, Haluka's cream, the Faste Winter and Ulfhild's account are Living Server lore.

story:
Thidranki was a farm before it was a field, and it was the first of the four the realms found open.

Midgard's skalds say that a northman's grandson named Thidrand kept the farm on the hill where the Faste stands now, and that he was killed in his own homefield on the winter nights by nine riders in black, while nine in white came on from the south too late to save him. The household left the hill the next spring. Albion remembers no farm, and says only that its squires pushed their first ram up that hill. Hibernia makes no claim on the farm, and says that a house which keeps two kinds of spirit will end by losing both.

It kept two. The tomte came over the water with the northmen, small grey spirits who mind the beasts and punish a careless farmer. The bwca were on the hill before them, shaggy house-spirits who do the night's work for a bowl of cream and turn on a household that forgets to set it out. With no farmer left, the two have quarrelled over the farm ever since, and both take the realms' soldiers for poor substitutes. The eldest bwca, Haluka, still keeps his corner below the Hibernian portal keep, twice the size of the rest.

Somebody raised the Faste over the old longhouse, and renegades held it when the realms came. In the second winter all three realms marched on it in the same week without knowing the others were coming, and the renegades went out by the back gate in the snow. The Faste has belonged to whoever took it last ever since, and its walls have worn more realms' colours than any keep in the world.
legend: Thidranki is the 20-24 battleground and the busiest of the four, the classic one, where most characters first fight over a keep that matters. Thidranki Faste in the middle has no renegade chieftain; it belongs to whoever took it last, so it changes hands a lot. The siegemasters at each portal keep (Salendar and Cadman for Albion, Ordrand and Sigfreid for Midgard, Camey and Erinden for Hibernia) sell rams and the like, and there are Void Merchants at the Midgard and Hibernia portal keeps. The tomte and the bwca attack anyone, and the bwca wander, so watch your back when you rest out in the fields. Haluka, the big bwca by the Hibernian portal keep, is level 24 and twice the size of the others; Hibernians meet him on their first day. Players call the field Thid and swear it was better in the old days.

firstEntry: A hill of old fields gone to grass, with a keep on top.

Thidranki. The oldest of the fields.

loremaster.intro: Thidranki, the oldest of the proving fields, and a [farm] once. Ask me of the [tomte], the [bwca] and [Haluka], of the [Faste Winter], or of [Thidranki Faste] and its [siegemasters].

topics.farm: A longhouse on a hill, with cattle and two kinds of spirit, the [tomte] and the [bwca]. Midgard says a northman's grandson kept it; Albion does not remember it; Hibernia makes no claim on it. The household left the hill and the spirits did not.
topics.tomte: Small grey farm spirits of the north who mind the beasts and punish a careless farmer. With no farmer left they hunt and soldier across the hill, and their visionaries watch the long grass as if somebody were expected.
topics.bwca: Shaggy house-spirits who do a farm's night work for a bowl of cream and turn on a household that forgets to set it out. Thidranki's have nobody to work for, and they roam. Their eldest is [Haluka].
topics.haluka: The eldest bwca of Thidranki, twice the size of the others, who keeps one corner below the Hibernian portal keep and does not wander. The druids say he is waiting for the household to come back with his cream.
topics.faste winter: The second winter of the fields, when all three realms marched on [Thidranki Faste] in the same week, each without knowing the others were coming. The renegades went out by the back gate in the snow while the three rams stood at the front one.
topics.thidranki faste: The keep on the crown of the hill, raised by somebody over the old longhouse. It has had no lord since the [Faste Winter], and belongs to whoever took it last.
topics.siegemasters: Each realm keeps siegemasters at its Thidranki portal keep: Salendar and Cadman for Albion, Ordrand and Sigfreid for Midgard, Camey and Erinden for Hibernia. Thidranki is where the young first learn that a keep can be taken.

book.title: The Farm under the Faste, as Ulfhild Long-Memory, skald of Mularn, set it down
pages: I have sung Thidrand's farm at three funerals, and I set it down now before I lose a verse. The farm stood on the hill where the Faste stands. The grandfather came over the water with his cattle and his tomte, and found a bowl of cream already set out on a stone, with nobody near it, and he had the sense not to drink it. The cream was for the bwca, who were on the hill before him, and he let them keep their corner. In his grandson's time it was a good farm. The beasts were minded and the night's work was done, and the household forgot neither kind of spirit.

Then came the winter nights on which Thidrand went out to the knocking, and in the spring the household left the hill, and the spirits did not. A tomte without a farmer has nobody to punish but strangers. A bwca without his cream turns on whoever is nearest. They have blamed each other for the farm ever since and fought over it in the long grass, and the young we send there are only the latest strangers. The eldest bwca sits in his corner below the Hibernians' gate and does not fight anyone he can wait out.

I was at the Faste in the second winter. We came up the hill in the snow with our ram, and found Albion's ram already at the gate and Hibernia's coming up the far slope, and none of us had known. The renegades went out by the back gate while we stood looking at each other. Nobody has held the Faste long since then. The tomte watched us take it that day without any interest at all. A keep is not a farm, and we are not the farmer.

midgard.story: Midgard tells Thidranki as its own. The farm was a northman's, and the tomte came over the water in his ship, and his grandson Thidrand was the last of the household to die on that hill. The skalds of Mularn sing it at funerals. Midgard's recruits leave a little porridge out for the tomte before they ride, as their grandmothers did for the tomte at home, and say it is only good manners. The tomte attack them all the same, and the skalds hold that a tomte's manners are his own affair.

loremaster.intro: Thidranki is Midgard's, whatever the others tell you. The first of the proving fields was a farm, and the farmer's son was [Thidrand]. The [tomte] came over the water with his grandfather; the [bwca] were on the hill before them, and the eldest, [Haluka], is there yet. The Faste on the longhouse has had no lord since the [Faste Winter].

topics.thidrand: Thidrand kept the farm on that hill, and he was eighteen, well liked, and courteous to a fault. On the winter nights a seer at the feast said that nobody should go out, whoever knocked. Someone knocked three times, and Thidrand went out because it was shameful to leave a guest at the door, and nine riders in black killed him in his own homefield while nine in white came on from the south too late. The seer said both were spirits of the house: the black taking their due before a change, the white belonging to what was coming. The skalds have never agreed what the change was. The women of Mularn say it was the fields.

albion.story: Albion remembers no farm at Thidranki and does not much care for the skalds' account of one. Its captains tell Thidranki as the hill where Albion's young learned siegecraft: the first ram an Albion squire ever pushed against a keep was pushed up that slope, and Siegemaster Salendar's family has kept the realm's rams at the southern gate since. Albion does claim the bwca, which are spirits of its own hills, and holds that they prove the farm was Albion's before a northman moved onto it.

loremaster.intro: Thidranki is the oldest of the proving fields, and the northmen say there was a [farm] on it, which may be so; Albion remembers only the hill. It was up that hill that an Albion squire first pushed a ram against a wall, and our [siegemasters] have kept the realm's siege gear at the southern gate ever since. The keep on the crown is [Thidranki Faste]. The grey things in the grass are [tomte], and the shaggy ones are [bwca], which are ours, whatever the skalds say.

topics.bwca: The bwca is a house-spirit of Albion's own hills, known from the Black Mountains to the sea, that does a farm's work by night for a bowl of cream and turns on a house that forgets to set it out. That there are bwca on the hill at Thidranki is the best proof that the farm was Albion's before ever a northman moved onto it, and the skalds have never answered it. The eldest of them is [Haluka]. He has been waiting for his cream a very long time, and he is in no mood to discuss whose he is.

hibernia.story: Hibernia makes no claim on Thidranki and is content to let the others quarrel over it. The druids say only that a house which keeps two kinds of spirit will end by losing both, and that the farm on the hill did. Hibernia's young meet the eldest of the bwca on their first day in the field, because his corner lies below their own gate, and the druids teach them to give him the respect due to an old neighbour who has been badly treated.

loremaster.intro: Thidranki, the oldest of the proving fields. It was a [farm], and the northmen will tell you whose, and the Albions will tell you otherwise. Hibernia makes no claim on it. A house that keeps two kinds of spirit, the [tomte] and the [bwca], will end by losing both, and so it did; and the eldest of the bwca, [Haluka], sits below our own gate to this day, waiting on a bowl of cream nobody has brought him.

topics.haluka: Haluka is the eldest of the bwca of Thidranki, twice the size of the rest of them, and he keeps the one corner below our gate and will not stir from it. Every young Hibernian meets him on their first day in the field, and most of them meet him again on their second, from the floor. The druids say he is waiting for the household to come back and set out his cream. Some of the young ones have tried leaving a bowl for him. He has never once touched it, which the druids say is only right, since it was not set out by the household.
